newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin leaves for NATO signing with warning.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin leaves for NATO signing with warning.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin left for Paris on Monday to sign a historic accord with NATO, warning the West that the deal would remove the risk of confrontation only if former Soviet republics dropped plans to join the alliance.

Russian television showed Yeltsin waving to officials before boarding his plane for the French capital, where he will sign a Founding Act with NATO leaders on Tuesday designed to put relations between the former Cold War foes on a new footing.

"This way we will not slip towards confrontation, which would inevitably involve big expenses for arms, a new militarisation of political thinking," the Russian president said in an interview published by the Kremlin on Monday.
Yeltsin, 66, hopes the accord will help him go down in history as the man who built the foundations of a secure and prosperous Russian state from the ashes of the Soviet Union.

But the loss of superpower status still stings in Russia and NATO's plan to issue invitations to some of Moscow's former allies this July in the face of fierce Russian opposition has only rubbed salt into the wound.
Yeltsin made clear in Monday's interview that Russia still saw NATO expansion as a big mistake despite the accord. "It is fraught with the risk of destabilising Europe," he said.

Anxious not to appear to be capitulating to the West, he also issued a warning to the alliance that their friendly relations with Russia would only hold if former Soviet republics could be persuaded to stay clear of NATO.
The Baltic states Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia are keen to join the alliance and Moscow is angered by NATO's refusal to rule out future membership for them.
"I hope that through an open dialogue we will be able to convince those and other countries that their security will not increase by bringing them closer to NATO," Yeltsin said.
"I do not even allow a thought that such a dialogue would fail. This would fully undermine relations between Russia and NATO," Yeltsin said.

Moscow has already made clear it would reconsider the accord if the West was tempted to "play Russian roulette", as Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky put it, comparing a NATO approach to any former Soviet republic with the deadly shooting game.

The alliance is expected to issue the first invitations to three former Warsaw Pact states outside the old Soviet Union -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic -- at a summit in the Spanish capital Madrid in July.
Yeltsin declined to specify whether or not he planned to attend the summit, saying he would have to see how future consultations with the alliance progressed.

Insisting that the accord protected Russian interests, he said it contained binding guarantees that NATO would not deploy nuclear weapons or build up its forces on the territory of the new members it takes in from the former Soviet bloc.
"We managed to secure in the document an obligation, I stress obligation, that such weapons would not be posted there and there would be no preparations to do so," he said.
"There is firm understanding that there will be no build-up of the forces of the alliance or any additional permanent stationing of NATO forces near our borders," Yeltsin said.
He said the deal created a mechanism for consultations and cooperation. "It allows, on a equal basis, joint consideration and resolution of the questions of security in Europe."
But NATO stopped short of promising Russia not to move military forces onto the territory of new members and has said Moscow will not have a veto over alliance decision-making.
In a sign the accord would not end Russia's efforts to win a more favourable reform of Europe's security architecture, Yeltsin held out hope for an alternative to the bi-polar system.

"The alternative is in creating a general and sweeping security system for the whole of Europe which will take into consideration security interests of every state, irrespective of its size, geographic position, economic or military potential."
